title: Stopping Steroids for Arthritis: When a Taper Is Needed
meta_title: Steroid Tapers and Arthritis: Safe Stopping Plans
meta_description: Do all steroid courses need a taper? Understand short-course exceptions, withdrawal symptoms, adrenal risk, sick-day plans and when to get urgent help.
excerpt: Some short steroid courses stop without a taper. Longer or repeated treatment needs an individual plan, clear illness precautions and review of new symptoms.
direct_answer: A steroid taper is not always needed, but the decision belongs to your prescriber. Some short courses have a stop date; repeated or longer treatment and adrenal risk may need gradual reduction. Flare, withdrawal and cortisol deficiency can cause overlapping symptoms. Follow your written plan and get urgent help for severe illness or a suddenly hot, swollen joint.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: steroid taper arthritis, stopping prednisolone, glucocorticoid withdrawal, adrenal insufficiency, steroid sick day rules
content:
First check: when symptoms need urgent help

This guide is for adults taking corticosteroids, such as prednisolone, for arthritis or another inflammatory condition. It explains the decisions behind a reduction plan, not a dose schedule. It does not apply to stopping life-essential steroid replacement for diagnosed adrenal insufficiency.

  • Call 999 for collapse, loss of consciousness or a suspected adrenal crisis. If you have adrenal insufficiency, have been told you are at risk, or become suddenly severely unwell during or after steroid treatment, severe weakness with marked dizziness, severe tummy pain, vomiting or confusion may need emergency assessment. Tell the ambulance team about current and recent steroid use. Do not drive yourself to A&E.
  • Use a prescribed emergency steroid injection if your plan says to and you have been trained, then still call 999. Do not wait to see whether the injection works before getting help.
  • If you have adrenal insufficiency and cannot keep steroid medicine down, seek immediate medical help. Prolonged vomiting or diarrhoea can prevent absorption. Follow your emergency plan; hospital treatment may be needed. Do not wait for the next routine appointment or invent a replacement dose from this article.
  • A suddenly very painful, hot or swollen joint needs urgent assessment now. Contact an urgent GP service or NHS 111, especially if you cannot move it, cannot bear weight or feel unwell. Joint infection can occur without fever. Do not assume it is a flare caused by reducing steroids.

NHS 111 is an urgent-advice route in England, Scotland and Wales. In Northern Ireland use your GP or GP out-of-hours service. Use 999 for an emergency anywhere in the UK.

The short answer: a taper is not always needed

Some short steroid courses have a prescribed stop date with no gradual reduction. Others need a taper, including some short courses when there has been repeated or recent longer treatment. Follow the plan written for you. If the label and the plan disagree, or no stopping instructions were given, check with the prescriber or pharmacist before changing the dose.

The 2024 European Society of Endocrinology and Endocrine Society guideline suggests that courses shorter than three to four weeks generally do not need tapering to prevent adrenal suppression. That is a guideline recommendation with low-certainty evidence, not personal clearance to stop. The UK prednisolone product information lists reasons to consider gradual withdrawal even after a short course, including repeated courses, recent long-term treatment, high doses and other causes of adrenal suppression. Your arthritis may also still need treatment.

NICE guidance covers withdrawal after longer exposure and says the clinical team who started treatment should make taper decisions. There is no single duration rule that replaces your treatment history, diagnosis and written prescription.

Why reducing steroids can be difficult

Corticosteroids reduce inflammation, but they can also suppress the body's usual cortisol production. Cortisol helps the body cope with illness and physical stress. After longer treatment, recovery can take time and differs between people. Taking longer to reduce is not a personal failure.

Three problems can overlap:

  • The underlying disease returning: arthritis inflammation may become active again as treatment falls.
  • Glucocorticoid withdrawal symptoms: fatigue, aches, low appetite or low mood can happen during reduction, even before the dose is low enough for cortisol deficiency to be the main concern.
  • Adrenal insufficiency: the body may not yet make enough cortisol, particularly at low doses, after stopping, or during illness when more cortisol is needed.

The joint endocrine guideline explains that symptoms overlap. You cannot reliably distinguish these problems from a symptom checklist at home. New or worsening symptoms need clinical review rather than being dismissed as expected withdrawal. Severe symptoms belong in the urgent section above.

What a useful taper plan contains

Reduction of long-term anti-inflammatory steroids should start when the underlying disease is controlled and steroids are no longer needed at that dose. The early part of a reduction and the final low-dose part may move at different speeds. Your team may slow, pause or change the plan after reviewing symptoms. Do not copy a friend's schedule or a dose chart from a different condition.

Before the next step, ask for:

  • the exact medicine, tablet strengths, daily instructions and date of each planned change;
  • who to contact about returning joint symptoms, side effects or difficulty following the plan;
  • what to do if symptoms develop before the next appointment;
  • enough tablets and the right strengths to avoid an unplanned stop;
  • a review date, illness instructions and any steroid-card advice.

Record your actual dose, the date of changes, new symptoms and what they stop you doing. Bring the record to review. Do not make an extra reduction, double a missed dose, restart leftovers or switch steroid medicines yourself. If you have missed doses or run out, get prompt advice from your pharmacist or prescriber; get emergency help if you are severely unwell.

Blood tests are a clinical decision, not a home stopping test

Not everyone needs a cortisol blood test to come off steroids. In adults, NICE advises considering a morning cortisol test in a particular situation: a slower taper has been tried and symptoms suggest adrenal insufficiency. The joint endocrine guideline also discusses either monitored tapering or morning cortisol testing near the body's usual replacement-level dose. These approaches are not a promise that everyone should be tested.

If your team requests a test, ask them exactly when to take or temporarily hold your medicine and when to restart it. Do not skip steroids to arrange a test yourself or interpret a result as permission to stop. The test timing, steroid type, laboratory method and clinical situation affect interpretation. Some people need endocrine advice, but most routine reductions can be managed by the treating team.

Illness, operations and the period after the last tablet

Adrenal recovery may lag behind the last tablet. Ask how long your precautions apply and when recovery has been established. Tell healthcare professionals about recent as well as current steroid treatment before surgery, invasive procedures or emergency care.

Give your team a complete list of steroid exposure, including inhalers, nasal sprays, creams and joint or muscle injections. Using several forms, recent injections and some interacting medicines can affect risk. A tablet-only history can miss relevant exposure.

If you have adrenal insufficiency or are at risk, get written sick-day rules and emergency instructions. The plan should cover fever or significant illness, vomiting or diarrhoea, surgery, whom to call and whether you need an emergency kit. Do not assume the answer is always to double the dose: it depends on the medicine and current treatment. If you cannot absorb oral steroids, follow the emergency plan and seek immediate help.

Ask whether you need a blue steroid treatment card, a red NHS Steroid Emergency Card, or both. Carry cards you are issued and show them to clinicians. A carer should know where the plan and any emergency kit are kept.

Keep the arthritis plan in view

For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE recommends short-term steroids for flares and considering them while a new conventional DMARD starts working. Repeated courses or difficulty reducing should prompt a review of longer-term disease control. Long-term use is not automatically wrong, but the benefits, complications and other options need a clear discussion.

key_takeaways: Not every short course needs a taper. Follow your own prescription and check unclear stopping instructions before changing the dose.
Flare, withdrawal symptoms and adrenal insufficiency overlap. New symptoms need review; collapse or a suspected adrenal crisis needs 999.
Ask about written illness rules, steroid cards, recent injections and how long precautions apply after the last tablet.
